opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to separate a few layers, because "AI for research" means very different things depending on which part of the research loop you're talking about.

Right now we're mostly at the stage where AI is a very good assistant for well-scoped subtasks: writing code, doing literature search, fitting a model, checking a derivation. That's useful, but the human is still doing the hard part, which is deciding what question is worth asking and judging whether an answer is actually interesting. So the first step toward automation at scale is closing the loop on smaller, verifiable problems. In fields where you can check results cheaply, like parts of math with formal verification, symbolic regression, or simulation-based physics, you can let the system propose a hypothesis, test it, and iterate without a human in every step. That's where I expect real autonomy to show up first, because the feedback signal is clean.

The second layer is something I care about a lot from my work on interpretability and things like KANs: the outputs have to be understandable. If an AI system discovers something but it's encoded in a billion parameters, it hasn't produced science in the traditional sense. It's produced a prediction tool. For research to scale, we need AI to produce compact, human-readable artifacts: formulas, conservation laws, mechanisms. Then humans can build on them, and other AI systems can too. Knowledge has to be compressible and composable, otherwise every discovery is a dead end.

The third layer, and I think the hardest, is taste. What makes a good scientist isn't just solving problems, it's picking problems, knowing when a weird result is a bug versus a discovery, knowing when to abandon a direction. That's very hard to put into a reward function. My guess is we'll get there gradually, by having AI systems run many small research projects, accumulating a track record, and learning from which directions turned out fruitful. Sort of like how a PhD student develops taste through many failed projects.

So the path I imagine is: start with domains that have cheap verification, insist on interpretable outputs so knowledge accumulates, and then slowly expand into more open-ended territory as the systems develop something like scientific judgment. Infrastructure matters too: standardized environments, benchmarks that reward discovery rather than just reproduction, and tooling that lets agents run experiments safely. I don't think it'll be one big leap. It'll look more like the scope of what we trust AI to do on its own steadily getting wider.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, it's great to be here.

I think the honest answer is that we're still very early, and the path to scale isn't a single leap. It's more like three stages that have to happen in order.

Right now, most of what people call "AI for research" is really AI as a very good assistant. It helps you write code faster, search literature, maybe suggest a hypothesis or two. But the human is still doing all the critical judgment: deciding what question matters, deciding whether a result is real or an artifact, deciding when to stop. That's the first stage, and we're mostly there.

The second stage, which I think we're just entering, is where AI can run a closed loop on a narrow, well-defined problem. You give it a clear objective, a simulator or an experimental setup it can call, and some notion of what counts as success. It proposes, tests, observes, revises. This works today in places like symbolic regression, some materials discovery, parts of mechanistic interpretability, where the feedback signal is cheap and unambiguous. The bottleneck here isn't intelligence. It's infrastructure. Research environments are messy. Most scientific code wasn't built to be called by an agent ten thousand times. So a lot of the near-term progress is unglamorous: making tools, data, and evaluation legible to machines.

The third stage, true automation at scale, requires something harder, which is taste. Knowing which problems are worth working on. Knowing when a surprising result is a discovery versus a bug. Knowing when to abandon a direction. Humans develop this over years, often through failure, and it's mostly tacit. I don't think we get there by scaling the current recipe alone. I think we need AI systems that can form and maintain their own models of a scientific field, notice anomalies against that model, and have some persistent memory of what they've tried and why it didn't work.

There's one more thing I'd add. I used to think of this as "replace the scientist." I now think the more realistic and frankly more interesting framing is that the unit of research changes. Instead of one person running one experiment at a time, you have a human directing a population of agents exploring a hypothesis space in parallel, and the human's job shifts toward asking better questions and interpreting what comes back. The scale comes from parallelism and from removing the drudgery, not from the AI suddenly having a genius insight.

So if I had to summarize: fix the plumbing first, build closed loops in domains with clean feedback, and in the meantime work seriously on the problem of taste, because that's the thing that actually separates doing experiments from doing science.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish automating a task from automating the research process. Right now, AI can help with individual steps—writing code, analyzing results, or proposing an idea. But a research project is a loop: you formulate a question, design an experiment, interpret what happened, and decide what to do next. To reach automation at scale, we need to connect those steps and make that loop reliable.

I would start with narrow settings where experiments are cheap and feedback is clear. Can the system produce a result that we can independently check? When an experiment fails, can it learn something useful and change direction? Once that works, we can gradually give it more open-ended problems.

The difficult part is deciding what is worth investigating. Running a thousand experiments is useful only if those experiments help us understand something. So I think humans will initially provide the questions and judgment, while AI handles more of the execution. Over time, AI can take a larger role in choosing the questions too—but that should follow demonstrated scientific progress, rather than simply the ability to generate more output.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make the research loop work, rather than just make one part of it faster. Right now, AI can help you read papers, write code, or analyze results. But a researcher still connects those pieces: deciding what question matters, choosing an experiment, interpreting a failure, and deciding what to try next.

To move toward automation at scale, we need environments where AI can go through that loop and get reliable feedback. In mathematics, you might have a proof checker. In some computational sciences, you can run a simulation and test a prediction. Those are good places to start because the system has a way to discover that its idea is wrong.

But checking an answer is only part of research. You also need to choose useful questions. An automated system could generate thousands of technically correct results that nobody cares about. So I would initially keep humans involved in setting the direction and judging significance, while letting AI take on longer sequences of experiments.

Then you expand the scope as the systems become reliable. Can it reproduce a known result? Can it resolve a small uncertainty? Can it propose and validate something unexpected? I think progress through those stages will tell us much more than whether an AI can produce a convincing research paper. The important thing is whether it produces knowledge we can trust and build on.
